questions.statement: Which element of the page most directly supports the claim in the caption?
questions.context: A page shows a bar chart of rainfall by month, a photograph of the reservoir, and a caption reading: 'Levels reached their lowest point in March.'

options.text: The bar chart, because it shows the monthly distribution of rainfall
options.feedback: A month-by-month distribution identifies March as a distinct point, which is exactly what the caption asserts.

options.text: The photograph, because it shows the appearance of the water
options.feedback: A photograph shows a moment visually but cannot establish which month the level was lowest.

options.text: The title of the page, because it names the subject
options.feedback: A title names the subject and carries no month-by-month data.

options.text: The footnote, because it explains the sources
options.feedback: A footnote explains provenance and does not supply evidence about levels.

questions.explanation:
A multimodal page is read by asking what each element can and cannot show. Matching a claim to the element that has the resolution to support it is the core skill.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does this statement matter to a reader?
questions.context: An article contains a chart, and the text beside it says: 'The chart does not include data for the years 2020 and 2021.'

options.text: Any trend the chart appears to show may be affected by those two missing years
options.feedback: A gap in the series can change how a trend appears, so a reader cannot read the shape without noting it.

options.text: The chart is unreliable in every other respect
options.feedback: The statement concerns two specific years and says nothing about the rest.

options.text: The two years had no rainfall at all
options.feedback: Absence of data is not the same as absence of rainfall.

options.text: The chart was withdrawn from publication
options.feedback: No withdrawal is mentioned anywhere in the text.

questions.explanation:
Notes placed beside a chart or table are instructions for interpretation. Reading them before the data is one of the habits that separate careful analysis from quick visual reading.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What must a reader check before comparing two districts on the map?
questions.context: An infographic shows a map with districts shaded in five tones, and the legend labels each tone from lowest to highest.

options.text: That the two districts are shaded with tones that are adjacent in the legend
options.feedback: Five tones classify values into bands, so a difference between two districts means different amounts only within a band.

options.text: That both districts appear in the legend
options.feedback: Every tone on a classified map corresponds to a legend entry, and membership is not the variable question.

options.text: That the map was printed in colour
options.feedback: The tone can be read in monochrome as distinct patterns, so printing is not the issue.

options.text: That the two districts have the same population
options.feedback: Nothing in the map classification depends on population size.

questions.explanation:
Classified maps carry a hidden quantisation: they group values into bands. A reader who treats a difference between tones as a measured difference is reading more precision than the map provides.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What advantage does a table provide over prose for these figures?
questions.context: A webpage presents the same figures as a table, as a chart and as a paragraph of prose.

options.text: It allows values to be located and compared row by row
options.feedback: A tabular layout places values in fixed positions, which makes precise comparison fast and reliable.

options.text: It explains what the figures mean
options.feedback: Interpretation is what prose is best at, and the table alone does not supply meaning.

options.text: It shows why the figures matter to readers
options.feedback: A table does not explain significance; the accompanying prose is where that appears.

options.text: It hides the original data source
options.feedback: A source note, when present, becomes easier rather than harder to find in a table.

questions.explanation:
Each presentation format answers a different question: tables for lookup, charts for pattern, prose for meaning. Choosing the right one for a task is part of reading multimodal material.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What limitation of this photograph should a reader keep in mind?
questions.context: A photograph shows people queueing at a clinic. The caption beside it states: 'Queues at the clinic last Tuesday.'

options.text: It shows one moment and cannot establish how long the queue usually lasts
options.feedback: A photograph freezes a single instant, so any claim about duration exceeds what the image can support.

options.text: It cannot be trusted because it was taken at a clinic
options.feedback: The location is not a reason to distrust the image.

options.text: It shows the wrong day of the week
options.feedback: The caption supplies the day, and nothing suggests it is wrong.

options.text: It proves that the clinic is underfunded
options.feedback: A funding conclusion would require financial evidence that the text does not provide.

questions.explanation:
The mismatch between what an image shows and what a caption or headline asserts is a routine source of misleading information. This item trains the habit of asking what the medium can actually demonstrate.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the note allow the reader to do?
questions.context: An infographic shows three icons: a person, a house and a hospital, with the note: 'Each figure represents one thousand residents.'

options.text: Convert the number of icons into an approximate population count
options.feedback: With a scale given for the symbols, counting them yields a total of multiples of one thousand.

options.text: Determine the exact population of each district
options.feedback: Icons give a rounded figure, and exact counts require the underlying data.

options.text: Compare the districts by income
options.feedback: The note concerns population size and says nothing about income.

options.text: Identify the year the data were collected
options.feedback: No date appears in the note or anywhere else in the description.

questions.explanation:
Icons and symbols compress numbers, and a scale note restores the link to real values. Recognising the compression is what allows a reader to use an infographic quantitatively without over-reading it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most defensible reading?
questions.context: A chart and a sentence in the text give different figures for the same year. The sentence adds: 'The chart uses the earlier estimate.'

options.text: Both figures can be correct because they come from different sources
options.feedback: The note identifies a difference in vintage, which explains the discrepancy without any need for an error.

options.text: One of the two must be a mistake
options.feedback: The explanation supplied by the text removes the need to assume a mistake.

options.text: The sentence is correct and the chart must be discarded
options.feedback: The note explains the chart rather than invalidating it.

options.text: The figures cannot be compared because both are estimates
options.feedback: Comparisons of two vintages remain possible once the difference is known.

questions.explanation:
A discrepancy between two figures is a question about provenance until the provenance is known. This item trains the habit of looking for a source note before deciding that either figure is wrong.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What makes this video a suitable complement to the written paper?
questions.context: A video summary of a research paper runs for four minutes and shows each figure from the paper on screen as it is discussed.

options.text: It presents the same figures while showing the speaker's explanation of them
options.feedback: Showing the figures alongside the interpretation gives the reader both the evidence and the reasoning about it.

options.text: It covers the same material in fewer words than the paper
options.feedback: Summarising reduces detail rather than presenting the same material in fewer words.

options.text: It can replace the paper for anyone with limited time
options.feedback: A summary supports the paper but does not replace it, since the full method and data remain in the text.

options.text: It presents additional experiments that the paper omitted
options.feedback: The figures come from the paper, so no additional experiments are involved.

questions.explanation:
A good multimodal complement carries the same evidence in a different channel. Recognising that the figures are shared while the explanation is added is what distinguishes a complement from a substitute.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the main interpretive risk in this map?
questions.context: A map shows the route of a proposed road as a straight line across a region, and the legend contains a scale bar.

options.text: The straight line hides the terrain that a real route would have to follow
options.feedback: Schematic lines are a generalisation, and terrain can force any real road to deviate substantially from them.

options.text: The scale bar is too small to read
options.feedback: The scale bar is provided, which is precisely what makes the drawing readable.

options.text: The map shows too many districts
options.feedback: The number of districts is unrelated to the accuracy of the route.

options.text: The route is drawn in the wrong colour
options.feedback: Colour carries no correctness role in the drawing of a route.

questions.explanation:
Cartographic generalisation is unavoidable, and knowing where it happens prevents over-reading a line as a precise path. This item asks the student to see the abstraction built into the medium.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why must the reader consult the threshold panel?
questions.context: A dashboard displays four indicators, and each one is coloured green, amber or red according to a threshold set in a separate panel.

options.text: The colour alone does not reveal the value or the limit being judged
options.feedback: Colour encodes a judgement whose basis lies in the thresholds, so without them the colour cannot be interpreted.

options.text: The panel explains who built the dashboard
options.feedback: Authorship information does not help a reader interpret a particular colour.

options.text: The panel contains the raw measurements
options.feedback: Raw measurements belong to the indicators, not to a panel of thresholds.

options.text: The panel is optional and can be ignored
options.feedback: The thresholds define what the colours mean, so the panel is not optional.

questions.explanation:
Colour-coded displays separate the signal from the rule that produces it. A reader who cannot see the rule cannot judge whether a green result is good, only that the system called it green.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What might a reader conclude by mistake if the scales are not read?
questions.context: A graph uses two different vertical scales, one on the left for rainfall and one on the right for river level, drawn in the same size type.

options.text: That rainfall and river level rise and fall together in proportion
options.feedback: A reader who ignores the scales can align apparent movements and mistake a visual coincidence for a proportional relationship.

options.text: That the river level is always higher than rainfall
options.feedback: The units on two axes are not directly comparable, so no such ranking can be drawn.

options.text: That rainfall has no effect on the river
options.feedback: Ignoring the scales gives no basis at all for a claim of no effect.

options.text: That the two series were recorded in different years
options.feedback: The years concern the horizontal axis and are not affected by the vertical scales.

questions.explanation:
Dual-axis charts invite an error because both lines share one visual field. Reading the axis labels before the pattern is the reliable procedure, and this item explains why.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should a reader note about the events the text does not discuss?
questions.context: An article includes a timeline graphic with six events, and the text beside it discusses only the third and the sixth.

options.text: The author has selected which events to interpret, and the selection may itself carry a message
options.feedback: Which events receive interpretation is a choice made by the author, and examining that choice is part of reading critically.

options.text: The remaining four events are not part of the history
options.feedback: A graphic timeline records events whether or not the text discusses them.

options.text: The remaining four events are less important than the others
options.feedback: Judging importance is not what the absence of discussion establishes.

options.text: The timeline is incomplete and cannot be relied on
options.feedback: The timeline may well be complete; nothing suggests otherwise.

questions.explanation:
Selection is an editorial act. A reader who asks why two of six events were chosen can often learn more about the author's framing than from the events themselves.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which feature of this page should concern a reader who intends to rely on the figures?
questions.context: An interactive map allows the visitor to click a district and see a panel of statistics about it. The page contains no explanation of where the statistics come from.

options.text: The absence of any statement about the data source or the year of collection
options.feedback: Without provenance and a date, the figures cannot be evaluated or compared with anything else on the page.

options.text: The fact that the map requires clicking rather than showing everything at once
options.feedback: Interactivity is a navigation choice and says nothing about the quality of the figures.

options.text: The number of districts available to inspect
options.feedback: The number of districts is irrelevant to the reliability of any one panel.

options.text: The language used in the labels
options.feedback: Label wording has no bearing on what the numbers mean or how current they are.

questions.explanation:
Interactivity makes a display feel authoritative because it offers detail on demand. Asking for the source of that detail is the way to keep the authority grounded.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this discrepancy suggest?
questions.context: A text presents a table of figures and a bar chart of the same figures. The chart's longest bar corresponds to the year with the smallest figure in the table.

options.text: The chart may represent something other than the values in the table
options.feedback: A bar longest where the underlying figure is smallest indicates that the two are not encoding the same measure.

options.text: The table must be in the wrong order
options.feedback: Sorting the table differently would not change which value is smallest.

options.text: The chart is always more reliable than the table
options.feedback: Neither format is inherently more reliable; the discrepancy indicates a mismatch rather than a preference.

options.text: The figures were collected in two different years
options.feedback: The year of collection is not what the discrepancy points to.

questions.explanation:
Cross-checking two representations of the same data is the strongest verification available to a reader. This item sets up the check and asks what an anomaly of this kind means.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should the reader conclude?
questions.context: A report contains a photograph of a new facility, and the caption identifies it as 'the largest in the region'. A table on the same page gives areas for five facilities, and none of them is described as largest.

options.text: The caption's claim and the table do not agree, so the claim requires checking
options.feedback: A statement and the data on the same page that disagree create an internal inconsistency that must be resolved before the claim is used.

options.text: The table is incorrect because the caption is the more authoritative text
options.feedback: Neither element is automatically authoritative, so ranking them does not settle the conflict.

options.text: The caption refers to a different measurement from the one tabulated
options.feedback: A different measurement is one possible explanation, but the text does not say so, and the conflict stands until it is checked.

options.text: The facility does not exist
options.feedback: Nothing in the description suggests the facility is fictional.

questions.explanation:
Internal consistency between claim and data is the first test a reader applies to any document. This item combines that check with the appropriate caution about guessing at explanations.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the strongest reading of this graph?
questions.context: A news site publishes a graph produced by a commercial organisation with an interest in the policy under debate. The graph carries no source note.

options.text: Its figures require verification because the producer is interested and no source is named
options.feedback: An interested producer and an absent source note are two specific weaknesses that together justify seeking independent verification.

options.text: It should be disregarded completely because graphs cannot carry arguments
options.feedback: A graph can certainly express an argument, which is why its provenance matters.

options.text: It is reliable because a professional organisation produced it
options.feedback: Professional production signals technical competence but says nothing about the interests behind the figures.

options.text: It is unreliable because news sites rarely publish graphs
options.feedback: Publishing graphs is common practice and is not itself a reason to doubt one.

questions.explanation:
Evaluating a visual source uses the same criteria as evaluating any source: who produced it, what interest they have and whether the data can be traced. This item names those criteria rather than issuing a verdict on the graph.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the pairing of narration and on-screen text accomplish?
questions.context: A website presents a short video in which a person reads out the figures from a chart shown on screen. The same figures appear in the accompanying text.

options.text: It lets a reader hear the figures and confirm them visually at the same time
options.feedback: Hearing and seeing the same values together supports verification, since a reader can check one against the other.

options.text: It removes the need to read the accompanying text
options.feedback: The visual confirmation remains available, so the text is not made redundant.

options.text: It presents the figures twice for no purpose
options.feedback: The duplication serves a purpose for anyone who cannot read or cannot hear clearly.

options.text: It makes the figures easier to alter without detection
options.feedback: Duplication can complicate alteration, which is the opposite of the last option.

questions.explanation:
Redundant channels are used in public communication precisely because they increase access and verifiability. This item asks the student to see the design principle behind two representations of one fact.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What can and cannot be concluded from these two elements?
questions.context: A report shows a photograph of a damaged building and states in the text: 'Damage was limited to the roof.'

options.text: The photograph shows visible damage while the text asserts its extent, which the image alone cannot confirm
options.feedback: A photograph records what is visible from one position, and it cannot establish that no other damage exists.

options.text: The text is false, because the photograph shows worse damage
options.feedback: A photograph of visible damage does not by itself contradict a claim about the limit of that damage.

options.text: The photograph confirms the text completely
options.feedback: A single image cannot verify the full extent described in the text.

options.text: The photograph was taken after the repairs were completed
options.feedback: The description shows visible damage, so the repairs interpretation has no basis.

questions.explanation:
The final group of items tests whether a reader can hold a claim and an image side by side without letting either settle the other's question. That restraint is what separates reading a multimodal document from merely looking at it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should a reader do to verify the sentence against the graph?
questions.context: An article pairs a graph with the sentence: 'As shown below, the figure rose each year without interruption.'

options.text: Check each year in the graph for a rise, including any year in which the value stayed level or fell
options.feedback: A claim of uninterrupted rise is a statement about every point on the series, so each must be examined.

options.text: Confirm that the graph is colour-printed
options.feedback: The method of printing has no bearing on the values plotted.

options.text: Read the source note to see whether the graph is current
options.feedback: A source note establishes provenance but does not check whether each year rises.

options.text: Compare the graph with a photograph of the same period
options.feedback: A photograph cannot verify annual values in a graph.

questions.explanation:
Verification of a graph claim is a point-by-point operation. This item asks the student to describe that procedure, which is the most practical skill in the whole area.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What difficulty does this design create for the reader?
questions.context: A document combines a summary paragraph, a detailed table, two photographs and a graph, and it presents all of them with equal visual weight and no guidance about their relationship.

options.text: There is no signal about which element should be read first or what each one contributes
options.feedback: Equal weighting removes the hierarchy that tells a reader where to begin and what each element is for.

options.text: The document contains too much information to be usable
options.feedback: The difficulty is navigational rather than a matter of total information volume.

options.text: The reader will not be able to remember all of it
options.feedback: Memory capacity is not a property of the document's design.

options.text: The elements belong to different subjects and should not appear together
options.feedback: Combining material on one subject is normal practice and not itself a defect.

questions.explanation: Good multimodal design signals the role of each element through position, size or labelling. This final item asks the student to identify a structural absence, which is the most transferable observation in this area of reading.
questions.subject: ingles
